challenges.title: CompTIA A+ Computer Component Match
challenges.description: Identify components, check compatibility and connect symptoms to useful checks.

rounds.title: Identification · working memory
rounds.prompt: Match this memory-module illustration to its job. Names are supplied as an alternative to the drawing.
rounds.objective: Distinguish temporary working memory from persistent storage.

choices.label: RAM — temporary workspace for active programs
choices.explanation: RAM needs power to retain working data; save persistent data to storage.

choices.label: SSD — temporary workspace that loses saved files at power-off
choices.explanation: An SSD is persistent storage, not the volatile workspace shown.

choices.label: PSU — workspace for active programs
choices.explanation: A PSU supplies DC power; it does not hold program data.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Distinguish temporary working memory from persistent storage.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

rounds.title: Identification · power
rounds.prompt: Which component turns wall-outlet AC into the DC power a desktop uses?
rounds.objective: Identify the PSU’s AC-to-DC function.

choices.label: Power supply unit (PSU)
choices.explanation: The PSU converts the input AC to the DC outputs used by components.

choices.label: Graphics card (GPU)
choices.explanation: A GPU processes graphics; it consumes power rather than converting outlet AC.

choices.label: Network interface card (NIC)
choices.explanation: A NIC connects to a network; it does not convert outlet power.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Identify the PSU’s AC-to-DC function.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

rounds.title: Identification · storage
rounds.prompt: Match persistent storage with no moving parts to a component.
rounds.objective: Distinguish solid-state storage from mechanical storage and RAM.

choices.label: Solid-state drive (SSD)
choices.explanation: An SSD stores data with no moving mechanical parts.

choices.label: Hard disk drive (HDD)
choices.explanation: An HDD uses mechanical components; it is not the no-moving-parts match.

choices.label: RAM module
choices.explanation: RAM is working memory, not the persistent storage requested.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Distinguish solid-state storage from mechanical storage and RAM.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

rounds.title: Compatibility · memory
rounds.prompt: Specification card: desktop DDR4 DIMM slots; the manual approves the offered DDR4 capacity/speed. Match the compatible module.
rounds.objective: Use memory generation and form factor to check compatibility.

choices.label: Approved DDR4 desktop DIMM
choices.explanation: It matches both the stipulated desktop module type and supported generation.

choices.label: DDR5 desktop DIMM
choices.explanation: A newer DDR generation does not fit an older DDR socket. Similar appearance is insufficient.

choices.label: DDR4 laptop SO-DIMM
choices.explanation: The generation matches but the laptop module form factor does not match the desktop DIMM slot.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Use memory generation and form factor to check compatibility.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

rounds.title: Compatibility · expansion
rounds.prompt: Specification card: available PCIe x16 slot, adequate space and approved PSU connectors/wattage. Which graphics card matches this interface?
rounds.objective: Match an expansion card to the supported slot and stated power constraints.

choices.label: PCIe x16 graphics card
choices.explanation: The specified interface matches; the scenario also explicitly satisfies space and power.

choices.label: Legacy AGP graphics card
choices.explanation: AGP is a different, obsolete interface; it does not match a PCIe slot.

choices.label: Plain PCI graphics card
choices.explanation: Plain PCI and PCI Express are distinct interfaces.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Match an expansion card to the supported slot and stated power constraints.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

rounds.title: Symptoms · storage
rounds.prompt: A mechanical drive shows read failures and heavy disk activity. Which component should you investigate first, preserving data before replacement?
rounds.objective: Connect disk-related symptoms to a storage investigation without overdiagnosing.

choices.label: HDD and its storage path
choices.explanation: Disk symptoms justify investigating the HDD/path and protecting data; they do not prove a unique cause.

choices.label: GPU only
choices.explanation: Graphics processing does not explain the disk-read evidence.

choices.label: NIC only
choices.explanation: Network connectivity is not the failing operation in this scenario.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Connect disk-related symptoms to a storage investigation without overdiagnosing.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

rounds.title: Symptoms · memory
rounds.prompt: A memory diagnostic reports errors after a memory upgrade. Which component and installation should you check against the manual?
rounds.objective: Use diagnostic evidence to prioritize a RAM/installation check.

choices.label: RAM modules and seating/compatibility
choices.explanation: The test targets memory. Check the upgrade and installation; this alone does not isolate a particular stick.

choices.label: SSD capacity only
choices.explanation: Storage capacity is not the subsystem implicated by the memory diagnostic.

choices.label: NIC link speed only
choices.explanation: Link speed is unrelated to the reported memory-test errors.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Use diagnostic evidence to prioritize a RAM/installation check.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

rounds.title: Identification · networking
rounds.prompt: Match the component responsible for connecting a computer to an Ethernet network.
rounds.objective: Identify the NIC’s network-connectivity role.

choices.label: Ethernet network interface card
choices.explanation: A NIC provides the computer’s network interface.

choices.label: Power supply
choices.explanation: The PSU supplies power, not an Ethernet data interface.

choices.label: Graphics card
choices.explanation: The GPU handles display/graphics work, not Ethernet connectivity.

rounds.hint: Compare the component’s job with the requirement. Physical appearance alone does not establish compatibility.

examMappings.area: Hardware and hardware troubleshooting: Identify the NIC’s network-connectivity role.

rounds.success: The match is supported by the stated function or evidence; a symptom identifies a check, not an automatic replacement.

challenges.title: IP Routing: Follow the Packet
challenges.description: Build a justified packet journey: local delivery, routed delivery, then a different network.

rounds.title: Compare destination subnet
rounds.objective: Use the mask to decide local versus remote.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Compare /24 network IDs: both are 172.16.30.0, so the destination is on-link.
choices.explanation: The destination is local; the host selects the destination itself as the link-layer next hop.

choices.label: Send to the gateway because all traffic must use a router.
choices.explanation: A router is unnecessary when both hosts share the on-link subnet.

choices.label: Compare MAC addresses to determine the IP subnet.
choices.explanation: Subnet membership comes from IP addresses and masks, not MAC equality.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: The destination is local; the host selects the destination itself as the link-layer next hop.

rounds.title: Resolve the local destination
rounds.objective: Choose the correct ARP target with an empty cache.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: ARP for 172.16.30.3 because the local destination has no cached MAC.
ARP for 172.16.30.1 because it is the gateway.
choices.explanation: The destination is on-link, so the gateway is not the next hop.

choices.label: Broadcast the IP data packet instead of resolving a MAC.
choices.explanation: ARP is the resolution exchange; the unicast data packet is not made a broadcast.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.

rounds.title: Construct the Ethernet frame
rounds.objective: Distinguish local MAC endpoints from IP endpoints.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Build C-MAC → D-MAC around IP 172.16.30.2 → 172.16.30.3; they are different address layers.
choices.explanation: The frame contains the IPv4 packet; EtherType 0x0800 identifies IPv4.

choices.label: Set the frame destination to the gateway MAC.
choices.explanation: This local destination needs Host_D’s MAC, not the gateway’s.

choices.label: Replace the destination IP with a MAC address.
choices.explanation: IP and MAC fields are separate; a MAC is not an IP destination.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: The frame contains the IPv4 packet; EtherType 0x0800 identifies IPv4.

rounds.title: Forward through the switch
rounds.objective: Explain switching without decrementing IP TTL.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Forward the frame using the switch MAC table; the switch does not route this packet.
choices.explanation: Switch-L forwards the Ethernet frame without changing its MAC endpoints or IP TTL.

choices.label: Reduce TTL to 63 because every network device counts as an IP hop.
choices.explanation: An Ethernet switch is not a routed IP hop.

choices.label: Send the frame to the router regardless of destination MAC.
choices.explanation: The known destination MAC selects the local output port.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Switch-L forwards the Ethernet frame without changing its MAC endpoints or IP TTL.

rounds.title: Deliver to the destination
rounds.objective: Explain frame removal and local IP delivery.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Host_D checks the frame and accepts its own destination IP; it removes link encapsulation.
choices.explanation: Host_D receives the packet with TTL 64. IP endpoints remained C → D; no routed hop occurred.

choices.label: Forward to the gateway to reduce TTL before accepting local traffic.
choices.explanation: The packet is already at its destination; no router forwarding is needed.

choices.label: Save the frame as permanent RAM data.
choices.explanation: Frame reception and IP delivery are networking operations, not persistent storage.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Host_D receives the packet with TTL 64. IP endpoints remained C → D; no routed hop occurred.

rounds.title: Compare source and destination
rounds.objective: Use subnet comparison to choose a gateway.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: 172.16.10.0/24 differs from 172.16.30.0/24; select 172.16.10.1 as the host next hop.
choices.explanation: Host_A uses its default route while keeping final destination IP 172.16.30.2.

choices.label: ARP directly for remote 172.16.30.2 on the source LAN.
choices.explanation: The remote host is outside this broadcast domain.

choices.label: Rewrite the packet destination IP to 172.16.10.1.
choices.explanation: The gateway is the frame next hop, not the final IP endpoint.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Host_A uses its default route while keeping final destination IP 172.16.30.2.

rounds.title: Resolve the gateway
rounds.objective: Resolve a local next-hop MAC for a remote IP destination.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: ARP for 172.16.10.1 on the source LAN because the gateway cache entry is absent.
choices.explanation: Gateway e0 replies with MAC 02:00:00:00:10:01.

choices.label: ARP for 172.16.30.2 across the router.
choices.explanation: ARP resolution is local; ordinary routers do not forward this broadcast.

choices.label: Ask DNS for the gateway MAC.
choices.explanation: DNS resolves names, while ARP resolves local IPv4-to-MAC mappings.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Gateway e0 replies with MAC 02:00:00:00:10:01.

rounds.title: Send the first frame
rounds.objective: Construct a frame to the gateway while retaining IP endpoints.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Send A-MAC → e0-MAC with IP 172.16.10.2 → 172.16.30.2; the router is only the next hop.
choices.explanation: Switch-A forwards to Lab_A e0; the packet arrives at the router with TTL 64.

choices.label: Send A-MAC → C-MAC before learning any reachable next-hop MAC.
choices.explanation: Host_C’s MAC is not on Host_A’s Ethernet segment.

choices.label: Change source IP to the router before sending.
choices.explanation: No NAT is configured; the host’s source IP stays unchanged.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Switch-A forwards to Lab_A e0; the packet arrives at the router with TTL 64.

rounds.title: Look up the destination route
rounds.objective: Apply longest-prefix match rather than first/default route.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Remove the received frame; look up 172.16.30.2 and choose the matching /24 through e2.
choices.explanation: The connected 172.16.30.0/24 route wins. The destination itself is the next hop on e2.

choices.label: Choose the matching /16 because it appears broader and handles more hosts.
choices.explanation: The matching /24 is more specific than /16 or /0.

choices.label: Look up the source IP to select the destination exit.
choices.explanation: Forwarding uses the packet destination, not the original source.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: The connected 172.16.30.0/24 route wins. The destination itself is the next hop on e2.

rounds.title: Update the IPv4 header
rounds.objective: Explain router TTL reduction without NAT endpoint changes.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Reduce TTL 64 → 63 and update the IPv4 header checksum before forwarding.
choices.explanation: TTL is 63; IP endpoints remain 172.16.10.2 → 172.16.30.2. TTL zero would cause a drop instead.

choices.label: Keep the whole IP header unchanged because frames alone change.
choices.explanation: TTL and its header checksum change at a routed hop.

choices.label: Replace source and destination IPs with the router interface addresses.
choices.explanation: Without NAT the IP endpoints stay Host_A → Host_C.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: TTL is 63; IP endpoints remain 172.16.10.2 → 172.16.30.2. TTL zero would cause a drop instead.

rounds.title: Resolve the outgoing next hop
rounds.objective: Use the selected exit network for address resolution.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: ARP on e2 for 172.16.30.2 because it is on-link there and the router cache is empty.
choices.explanation: Host_C maps to 02:00:00:00:30:02 on e2.

choices.label: ARP on e0 for Host_A again.
choices.explanation: The source-side MAC does not provide the outgoing destination mapping.

choices.label: ARP for the remote host on every interface.
choices.explanation: The selected route determines which local network needs resolution.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Host_C maps to 02:00:00:00:30:02 on e2.

rounds.title: Rebuild and forward
rounds.objective: Explain which link-layer addresses change after routing.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Build e2-MAC → C-MAC around the same IP endpoints with TTL 63; forward on e2.
choices.explanation: The new frame has source 02:00:00:00:30:01 and destination 02:00:00:00:30:02; Switch-C forwards it.

choices.label: Reuse A-MAC → e0-MAC on the destination LAN.
choices.explanation: Those MAC endpoints belong to the previous Ethernet segment.

choices.label: Change destination IP to e2 because it constructs the frame.
choices.explanation: Constructing a frame does not replace the final IP destination.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: The new frame has source 02:00:00:00:30:01 and destination 02:00:00:00:30:02; Switch-C forwards it.

rounds.title: Deliver the routed packet
rounds.objective: Recognize destination delivery and end-to-end IP addresses.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Host_C accepts its own MAC/IP destination and delivers the packet; no further forwarding is required.
choices.explanation: Host_C receives IP 172.16.10.2 → 172.16.30.2 with TTL 63. Ethernet endpoints changed at the router, not at the switches.

choices.label: Decrease TTL again because the destination is another routed hop.
choices.explanation: Receiving the final packet is not forwarding it as a router.

choices.label: Report that Host_A’s IP changed because the Ethernet source changed.
choices.explanation: Frame-source MAC changed; the IPv4 source did not, because this scenario has no NAT.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Host_C receives IP 172.16.10.2 → 172.16.30.2 with TTL 63. Ethernet endpoints changed at the router, not at the switches.

rounds.title: Transfer: choose resolution behavior
rounds.objective: Apply a different subnet and a populated ARP cache.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Destination 10.10.2.70 is remote; use cached gateway 10.10.1.1 → 02:00:00:01:00:01.
choices.explanation: Source can construct its first frame from the valid gateway mapping, keeping IP destination 10.10.2.70.

choices.label: Broadcast ARP for 10.10.2.70 on the source /24.
choices.explanation: The destination is not on the source LAN.

choices.label: Always send a new ARP request even for a valid populated cache.
choices.explanation: This stated valid cache already supplies the mapping; no new request is needed.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: Source can construct its first frame from the valid gateway mapping, keeping IP destination 10.10.2.70.

rounds.title: Transfer: choose the route
rounds.objective: Apply longest-prefix match with /26 versus /24 and default.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: 10.10.2.70 falls in 10.10.2.64/26; choose e1 because /26 is the longest matching prefix.
choices.explanation: The on-link /26 supplies the outgoing interface. R2 uses its cached destination MAC.

choices.label: Choose 10.10.2.0/24 because it is the larger network.
choices.explanation: Larger address coverage is not a more specific route.

choices.label: Choose the default route before checking the /26.
choices.explanation: A matching /26 wins over /24 and /0.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: The on-link /26 supplies the outgoing interface. R2 uses its cached destination MAC.

rounds.title: Transfer: predict received addresses
rounds.objective: Predict TTL and both address layers on a different network.
rounds.prompt: Place the next step in the packet journey. Choose both the action and its justification.

choices.label: Send e1-MAC → destination-MAC; deliver IP 10.10.1.20 → 10.10.2.70 with TTL 63.
choices.explanation: R2 updates TTL/checksum, uses its warm ARP cache, and constructs a new frame. The destination receives the unchanged IP endpoints at TTL 63.

choices.label: Deliver with gateway source IP 10.10.1.1 and TTL 64.
choices.explanation: No NAT changes the source IP; the router also reduces TTL.

choices.label: Reuse the first frame MACs and decrement TTL at each switch.
choices.explanation: Router forwarding rebuilds the frame; Ethernet switches do not decrement IP TTL.

rounds.hint: Use the current packet location, subnet mask and cache state. A link-layer next hop can differ from the final IP destination.
rounds.success: R2 updates TTL/checksum, uses its warm ARP cache, and constructs a new frame. The destination receives the unchanged IP endpoints at TTL 63.

scenarios.title: Same subnet · Host_C to Host_D
scenarios.description: Host_C and Host_D share 172.16.30.0/24. Router e2 is the available gateway but is not required for local delivery.
scenarios.assumptions: IPv4 unicast over Ethernet; /24 masks unless shown otherwise; no NAT, VLAN changes, fragmentation, loss or ACL blocks; initial TTL 64. Switch MAC tables are populated. MAC addresses are authored locally administered examples. Decisions model conceptual order; implementations may overlap processing. Host_C ARP cache starts empty.

scenarios.title: Routed · Host_A to Host_C
scenarios.description: Source LAN 172.16.10.0/24 → Lab_A → destination LAN 172.16.30.0/24. The router also has e1 on 172.16.20.0/24.
scenarios.assumptions: IPv4 unicast over Ethernet; /24 masks unless shown otherwise; no NAT, VLAN changes, fragmentation, loss or ACL blocks; initial TTL 64. Switch MAC tables are populated. MAC addresses are authored locally administered examples. Decisions model conceptual order; implementations may overlap processing. Host_A and router e2 ARP caches start empty.
context: A broader fallback route is an authored exercise assumption; connected routes use Chapter 9 addresses.

scenarios.title: Transfer · a different network and warm ARP caches
scenarios.description: Authored network: 10.10.1.20/24 → R2 → 10.10.2.70/26. Apply the same principles to different prefixes.
scenarios.assumptions: IPv4 unicast over Ethernet; Source /24; destination LAN /26; no NAT, VLAN changes, fragmentation, loss or ACL blocks; initial TTL 64. Switch MAC tables are populated. MAC addresses are authored locally administered examples. Decisions model conceptual order; implementations may overlap processing. Source ARP cache has 10.10.1.1 → 02:00:00:01:00:01. R2 ARP cache has 10.10.2.70 → 02:00:00:02:00:70.
context: Ethernet switching between nodes is implicit in this compact transfer diagram.
